title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATES, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATINGS FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Water is a basic human need and access to safe water is a universal human right as declared by the United Nations. With global warming, water security is a growing problem worldwide, and it calls for long term planning and responses. In the case of the Philippines, although an archipelagic country blessed with an abundant source of water, severe water shortage is being experienced due to the impact of rapid population growth, urbanization, pollution, excessive and inefficient use of water, and climate change. This is further aggravated by the lack of a holistic program for water resources management. One of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) adopted by all United Nations Member States in 2015 is to ensure availability and sustainable management of water and sanitation for all by 2030.1 Despite progress, billions of people still lack safe water, sanitation and handwashing facilities. Data suggests that achieving universal access to even basic sanitation service by 2030 would require doubling the current annual rate of progress. At present, management of water resources in the country is lodged with different units or agencies of the government such as National Water Resources Board (NWRB), Local Water Utilities Administration (LWUA), Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS), and the National Irrigation Administration (NIA) thereby resulting to duplication of functions, lack of coordination or even conflicts in the implementation of the national policies and plans on water, sewage, sanitation, and irrigation thereby resulting to backlog in the provision of water supply and sanitation services to the public. 1 https://sustalnabledevelopment.un.org/sdg6 1 This bill seeks to ensure and accelerate universal access to water supply and sanitation services and to encourage responsible private sector participation, fostering and prioritizing infrastructure and public works that adopt innovative solutions and international best practices to address the challenges of climate change. The key provisions include the following: ● Creates, establishes, and mandates the Department of Water Resources to be the primary agency responsible for the comprehensive and integrated identification and mapping of all water resources, planning, policy formulation, and management of the ownership, appropriation, utilization, exploitation, development, sustainability and protection of water resources in the Philippines except fisheries or aquaculture; ● Declares all water and water treatment infrastructure projects as projects imbued with national interest; ● Adopts the Integrated Water Resource Management (IWRM) as the strategic framework for national water management, policymaking and planning; ● Empowers the Department on policy making, planning, management and regulation of water resources; and to develop institutional arrangements with public water organizations and ensure coordination with all stakeholders for all water resource development, integration and management activities, including sanitation, flood control, flood risk management and drought risk management; ● Empowers the Department to create when necessary, water resource subsidiaries, instrumentalities and entities to engage in water transmission, water distribution, waste water treatment and management, and sanitation in accordance with existing relevant laws; ● Allows the Department to enter into contracts, joint venture agreements or understanding, public-private partnerships, and memorandum of agreements or understanding, either domestic or foreign relating to investment and financing water-related projects, under such terms and conditions as the Department may deem proper and reasonable subject to existing laws; ● Authorizes the Secretary of the Department to act as the Chairperson of the governing board of the agencies that are attached to the Department; ● Attaches agencies to the Department as follows: 1. The Local Water Utilities Administration (LWUA); 2. The Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS); 3. The National Irrigation Administration (NIA); 4. The Laguna Lake Development Authority (LLDA), whose mandate, powers and functions are defined under Republic Act No. 4850; ● Subsumes the offices, functions and personnel of the following agencies to the Department, namely: 1. The National Water Resources Board (NWRB); 2. The River Basin Control Office (RBCO) of the DENR; 3. The 2 Manila Bay Coordinating Office (MBCO) of the DENR; 4. The Water Resources Management Division of the Bureau of Soils and Water Management of the Department of Agriculture (DA); 5. The Water Supply and Sanitation Unit of the DILG; 5. The Water Quality Management Section of the EMB of the DENR; and 6. The Water Quality Management Section of the Environmental Management Bureau (EMB) of the DENR; ● Transfers to the Department the functions of the following agencies, bureaus, and units: (1) The conduct of hydrological surveys and groundwater mapping of the Mines and Geosciences Bureau (MGB) of the DENR. (2) The conduct of hydrological surveys monitoring of stream flow and other water data collection function of the Bureau of Design and Bureau of Research and Standards of the DPWH. (3) The protection and conservation of natural wetlands such as lakes, marshes, swamps of the Biodiversity Management Bureau of the DENR. (4) The Planning, programming, administration, monitoring, management of the National Sewerage and Septage Management Program (NSSMP) by the DPWH. (5) The flood management planning and sediment management function of the Flood Control Management Cluster of the DPWH. (6) The Water Resource Management Division and the water research functions of the Soils and Water Research Division of the Bureau of Soils and Water Management under the DA. ● Creates the Water Pollution Adjudication Board to assume the powers and functions of the National Pollution Control Commission with respect to the adjudication of water pollution cases;

explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to rationalize the water, irrigation, sewage, and sanitation resource management, including water rights, through the creation of the Department of Water, Irrigation, Sewage, and Sanitation Resource Management. Water is a basic human need and access to safe and clean drinking water is a basic human right as recognized by the United Nations. As a national water crisis looms according to a study by the Japan International Cooperation Agency and the Philippines' National Water Resources Board and all major cities of the Philippines have been foreseen to all suffer from water shortage by 2025, it is only imperative and necessary to take a much needed affirmative action to prevent this catastrophe1. The present set-up for water, irrigation, sewage, and sanitation responsibilities of the government involves, among others, the following major government agencies: a) National Water Resources Board (NWRB), a government agency responsible for the enforcement of the Water Code of the Philippines which is under the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR); b) Local Water Utilities Administration (LWUA), a government-owned and controlled corporation (GOCC) attached to the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) and has regulatory powers over: 1) all local water districts (LWDs); and 2) rural waterworks and sanitation associations (RWSAs) nationwide; c) Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS), a GOCC also attached to the DPWH, which is responsible for the water supply and sanitation in Metropolitan Manila and such contiguous areas as may be added to its area of jurisdiction, and; d) National Irrigation Administration (NIA), a government agency under the Office of the President primarily responsible for irrigation development and management. 1 Explanatory Note of SB 208 authored by Senator Francis Tolentino during the 18 th Congress entitled: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES MANAGEMENT DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES which was filed on 2 July 2019 This bill, therefore, seeks to create the Department of Water Resources Management which shall be the primary agency responsible for the comprehensive and integrated water resources development and management in the Philippines. Guided by the integrated water resources management framework and taking into account climate risks, the Department shall exercise such powers and functions needed to review, revise, harmonize and integrate policies and regulations for conservation of water resources and effective management of potable water supply. In managing water resources, the Department shall aim to improve water conservation, increase system efficiencies, and optimize the use of all freshwater in the country including ground water, surface water, rainwater, run-offs, floods and urban drainage, and treated wastewater to meet various needs. It must be stressed that the Philippine government’s responsibility to safe, clean, accessible and affordable drinking water, sanitation, and irrigation service to the public is of utmost importance and it is attainable through well-coordinated, effective, efficient and sustainable management of its water and sanitation resources. The proposed Department of Water, Irrigation, Sewage and Sanitation Resource Management shall have the following primary functions: 1) Set the policies for water supply and sewage and sanitation management; 2) Develop and manage the country’s water resources to ensure optimal use, including but not limited to, domestic, irrigation, power generation, industrial, agricultural, and commercial use; 3) Build, maintain and monitor water-related infrastructure, water quality and accessibility; 4) Regulate the operation and management of water utilities such as MWSS, LWDs, RWSAs and other water and sanitation service providers; 5) Make available and/or provide financial assistance to non-viable LWDs for the improvement of water facilities or services through funds prior and future appropriations of the National Government for waterworks and sewerage systems; 6) Regulate and control the utilization, exploitation, development, conservation and protection of all water resources; 7) Administer and enforce the provisions of Water Code of the Philippines; 8) Plan, design, construct, and/or improve all types of irrigation projects and appurtenant structures; 9) Operate, maintain, and administer all national irrigation systems (NIS); 10)Supervise the operation, maintenance, and repair, or otherwise, administer temporarily all communal and pump irrigation systems constructed, improved, and/or repaired wholly or partially with government funds; 10) Delegate the partial or full management of NIS to duly organized cooperatives or associations; 11) Construct multiple-purpose water resources projects designed primarily for irrigation, and secondarily for hydraulic power development and/or other uses such as flood control, drainage, land reclamation, domestic water supply, roads and highway construction, and reforestation, among others, Provided, that the plans, designs, and the construction thereof, shall be undertaken in coordination with the agencies concerned; 12) Charge and collect from the beneficiaries of the water from all irrigation systems constructed by or under its administration. Following the lead of other countries who have found it wise to create a special department to manage this vital resource of water including Japan, Australia, China, and India, the availability of potable water in the Philippines and the continuing water supply for domestic, agricultural and industrial consumption may be ensured and the perennial problem that seriously affects the lives of the people in terms of health, sanitation, food security, and livelihood may be effectively addressed. In view of the foregoing, approval of this measure is earnestly sought. KHYMER ADAN T. OLASO Representative 1s

The waters around, between, and connecting the islands of the archipelago, regardless of their breadth and dimensions, form part of the internal waters of the Philippines.” The Philippines, as an archipelagic country, is endowed with vast water resources, yet water shortage is felt all year round all over the country. Another challenge the Philippines faces is improper water waste treatment. During the 16th Water Environment Partnership in Asia (WEPA) Annual Meeting, it was reported that “only 10% of wastewater is treated.”, while “only 5% of the total population is connected to a sewer network.” On a larger scale, climate change has drastically affected water resources and these negative effects are especially felt during the El Nifio and La Nifa episodes. The burden falls upon the government to institute a water resources management system that effectively delivers safe and clean water to its constituents and provides for its proper treatment, disposal, and waste sanitation. Pursuant to Presidential Decree No. 1067 or the Water Code of the Philippines, there exists a National Water Resources Board (NWRB) vested with powers to nr” de Y, < RECEIVED ry fe + d o// coordinate and integrate water resources development. The NWRB, as an attached agency, is under the administrative supervision of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR). Proper water resources management could only result in positive repercussions for the simple Filipino citizens and the Philippine economy and environment. This bill seeks to create a Department of Water Resources Management, which shall ensure the maximum utilization of available water resources for the least costs possible while warranting equal distribution to Filipinos all over the country. A government that is able to provide even the most basic needs to its people is one that satisfies the principles of social justice. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines during the Global Forum on Water Supply and Sanitation, which was held in Manila in 1997, envisions “a world class, affordable and sustainable water supply, sanitation and sewerage system accessible to every Filipino”. It was conceived consistent with the long-term vision on water, life and the environment or World Water Vision 2025. In this light, it is imperative upon the government to develop a comprehensive national water resources management system to fully streamline the water sector and revitalize it in terms of the efficiency and sufficiency of its service and resources. Hence, the creation of the Department of Water, Irrigation, Sewage and Sanitation Resource Management as proposed in this bill seeks to rationalize the water, irrigation, sewage, and sanitation resource management, including water rights. Presently, the set-up of water, irrigation, sewage, and sanitation responsibilities of the government involves, among others, the following agencies: (1) National Water Resources Board (NWRB), an agency under the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) responsible for the enforcement of the Water Code of the Philippines; (2) Local Water Utilities Administration (LWUA), an attached agency to the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) which exercises regulatory power over all local water districts and rural waterworks and sanitation associations all over the country; (3) Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS), a government-owned-and- controlled corporation also attached to the DPWH that is responsible for the water supply and sanitation in Metropolitan Manila and such contiguous areas as may be added to its area of jurisdiction; and (4) National Irrigation Administration (NIA), a government agency under the Office of the President which is primarily responsible for irrigation development and management. In the face of fragmented regulation and management of water resources in the country, there have been chailenges in the coordination and implementation of the national policies and plans on water, sewage, sanitation, and irrigation, which has resulted in a backlog in the delivery of water supply and sanitation services to the public. It must be emphasized that government's responsibility to provide safe, clean, accessible and affordable drinking water, sanitation, and irrigation service to the public is of utmost importance and can be realized through well-coordinated, effective, efficient and sustainable management of its water and sanitation resources. This has even more become urgent in the face of the country’s rapid population growth, water pollution, watershed degradation, increasing agricultural requirements for food production, waterborne diseases, climate change, and other related factors that need to be adequately addressed without delay. The creation of the Department of Water, Irrigation, Sewage and Sanitation Resource Management will strengthen and coordinate water resource planning and policy-making to ensure sustainable and fair allocation and efficient use of water resources between water uses and users such as irrigation, power generation, and farming among others. Through this proposed agency, the immediate attainment of universal access to safe, adequate, and sustainable water supply and sanitation services for all Filipinos will be given priority. In view thereof, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. foe Keith Micah “Atty. Mike” D.L. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Along with climate change, water resources management is the next great global concern. The paradox of our time is that our planet’s surface is made up of 71% water yet so many places around the world are facing water shortage. This is because 96% of all water on earth is in the oceans and not for daily use. According to World Wildlife Fund’, “1.1 billion people lack access to water and 2.7 billion experience water scarcity at least one month a year. By 2025, two-thirds of the world’s population may be facing water shortages. When waters run dry, people can’t get enough to drink, wash, or feed crops, and economic decline may occur. In addition, inadequate sanitation——a problem for 2.4 billion people—can lead to deadly diarrheal diseases, including cholera and typhoid fever, and other water-borne illnesses.” In the Philippines, more than three million people rely on unsafe and unsustainable water sources and seven million lack access to improved sanitation” Current projections of climate up to 2050 suggest the Philippines will become warmer, with increasing temperature and decreasing rainfall during the dry season and more extreme rainfall events during the wet season. This will undoubtedly exacerbate both water availability during periods of drought and the magnitude of flood events during periods of heavy rainfall.? In addition to water stresses from a changing climate, the population is expected to increase by around fifty percent (50%) up to 2050, with the urban population set to double over the same period. This will further exacerbate pressures on future water resources.* " World Wildlife Fund (n.d.) Hater Scarcity. We are already feeling the effects of water shortage. !t ts not an infrequent occurrence for water companies to limit or ration water services during the dry season to ensure that enough supplies are available until the rainy season. Clean and potable water figures in all aspects of our future: from the health and survival of our people, to our food supply, to our agricultural and industnal development. Before it reaches a full crisis mode, there is an urgent need to establish a department with a mandate and ample resources that will be commensurate to the surmountable challenges that we will be facing. This early, we need to create an effective and sustainable water resources management program that will be resistant to the effects of climate change and sufficient to serve the needs of our developing and growing country. This measure establishes the Department of Water Resources Management whose task is to develop and implement programs and policies to promote universal access to safe, adequate, affordable, and sustainable water supply, irrigation, sewage, and sanitation services for all Filipinos. This bill likewise seeks to promote the use of rainwater harvesting facilities throughout our country to augment our water supply needs. Under this measure, the new Department is likewise mandated to protect all water resources with greater emphasis on sources of drinkable water and work closely with the Local Government Units (LGUs) for the protection of waters within their jurisdictions especially on pollution prevention and river restoration. Another provision under this bill also puts a spotlight on barangays as it transfers the supervision from the Department of Public Works and Highways to the new Department on the construction and operation of all wells and other water-harvesting facilities. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE While our country has been blessed with ample water sources, and bountiful rainwater during the wet months, these remain vulnerable to wastage and are not properly stored to serve us during the dry months. Moreover, it appears that the country continues to be confronted with multi-faceted issues like the reportedly dismal performance of water regulatory agencies, poor or no access to clean drinking water in many parts of our country, rising water rates— all of which are aggravated by climate change. Hence, it has become imperative that our government be made ready and able to carry out a timely and effective response at all times. Thus, this proposed measure, which is anchored and principally based on the remarkable output of the Committees on Government Reorganization, Public Works and Highways, Ways and Means, and Appropriations in the 18th Congress, seeks to rationalize the country’s water, sewage, and sanitation resource management, including water rights, through the creation of the Department of Water Resources and the Water Regulatory Commission. Through the concerted efforts of these critical agencies, it is envisioned that, among others, clearer and more organized policies for water supply and sanitation are established and that the country’s water resources are developed and managed to ensure its optimal use such as in irrigation, power generation, industrial, agricultural and commercial use. At this critical juncture in our country’s history where our people are still wary of the pandemic and are truly burdened with the global crisis on oil and fuel, we cannot succumb to a water crisis as well. In view of the foregoing, approval of this measure is earnestly requested. ROSANNA “RIA” V. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATES, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS,AND APPROPRIATINGS FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This measure supports the House leadership in its effort at aligning with the administration’s objective of ensuring the provision of safe, adequate, affordable, and sustainable water supply and improved sanitation services, while maintaining the protection, preservation, and revival of the quality of the country’s water resources and ecological balance. In order to do this, it is imperative to ensure and accelerate universal access to water supply and sanitation services, and to encourage responsible private sector participation. In addition, there is also a dire need to start establishing necessary infrastructure which would effectively support and innovate solutions aimed at addressing the problems on climate change. The United Nations has always recognized that access to safe and potable drinking water is a basic right. If we do not act on it as early as now, water scarcity, as predicted, will become a substantial problem in the foreseeable future. To void this predicament, we must begin with effective and coordinated administration and management of the country’s water resources. At present, there are over 30 government units and agencies, both at the national and local levels, which implement different projects and policies, mostly independent from one another. This inevitably results in confusion, thus, preventing systematic creation and implementation of solutions to rectify the situation. Indeed, there is an urgent need for an integrated and coordinated planning and implementationof programs and projects that would synchronize sustainable and science-based management of the country’s water resources. It is thus proposed that a Department of Water Resources and a Water Regulatory Commission be created to ensure that Filipinos will be accorded the fundamental human right to water. A similar measure was filed in the 18th Congress by Representative Estrellita Suansing. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT FOR THIS PURPOSE CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATES, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATINGS FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State is responsible for providing water security to all citizens and inhabitants of its country. The Philippines as a water-rich country needs to rationalize and streamline the implementation of its existing and sometimes overlapping policies, laws and regulations affecting its water resources including irrigation, sewage and sanitation. In President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s State of the Nation Address on 25 July 2022, the President called on Congress to pave the way for the creation of a Department of Water Resources to adopt an integrated water resource management and address the water supply issues in the country especially in the urban areas. The bill proposes to create the Department of Water Resources to serve as the primary agency responsible for national policy-making, coordination and management of all the water resources in the Philippines. All government agencies related to water shall be rationalized under this Department. Integrated Water Resources Management shall be adopted as the strategic framework for water management policy-making and planning in the country. The bill also proposes to create an independent Water Regulatory Commission to ensure the effective and adequate delivery of water and sanitation services throughout the country under a credible, transparent and accountable regulatory framework. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. LORENZ R. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In line with the streamlining efforts of the government bureaucracy under the current President BBM administration, there is an opportunity to provide an improved and effective management of our country’s water resources through the establishment of a Department of Water Resources. According to reports1, “more than 3 million people in the Philippines rely on unsafe and unsustainable water sources and 7 million lack access to improved sanitation. Despite its growing economy, the Philippines faces significant challenges in terms of water and sanitation access. The country is rapidly urbanizing, and its growing cities struggle to provide new residents with adequate water and sanitation services. In 2010, the government of the Philippines developed a road map to achieve universal water and sanitation services coverage by 2028. In the Philippines and around the world, people are navigating the COVID-19 pandemic, and millions are striving to endure this crisis with an added challenge. They lack access to life’s most critical resource – water. Now more than ever access to safe water is critical to the health of families in the Philippines.” There are various government agencies battling this recurring water and sanitation crisis and there is a need now more than ever to consolidate these efforts to avoid duplication of functions, improve public service delivery, and to prudently manage limited government resources to address this pressing concern. 1 https://water.org/our-impact/where-we-work/philippines/ (last accessed 08 August 2022) 1 Hence, the introduction of this Bill establishing the Department of Water Resources which shall serve as the lead agency to implement and regulate water-related programs, policies, and projects of the country. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER, IRRIGATION, SEWAGE, AND SANITATION RESOURCE MANAGEMENT, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to ensure sustainable, fair, and efficient use and allocation of water irrigation, sewage, and sanitation resources through the creation of the Department of Water Irrigation, Sewage, e, and Sanitation Resource Management. The Philippines, as an archipelagic country, is surrounded by numerous bodies of water. It is considered abundant in water resources “having been endowed with 59 lakes and 421 river basins with drainage area ranging from 40 to 25,649 sq. km.1” Considering this, the country should have an adequate supply for domestic, agricultural, and industrial purposes. However, with the water shortage brought about by the worsening effects of climate change and subsequent worsening of the El Niño season the state must account for the country’s water resources and address the growing problem of the country’s water supply. Presently, the management of our water resources involves numerous government agencies, namely: a) National Water Resources Board (NWRB), a government agency responsible for the enforcement of the Water Code of the Philippines which is under the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR); b) Local Water Utilities Administration (LWUA), a government-owned and controlled corporation (GOCC) attached to the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) and has regulatory powers over: 1) all local water districts (LWDs); and 2) rural waterworks and sanitation associations (RWSAs) nationwide; c) Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS), a GOCC also attached to the DPWH, which is responsible for the water supply and sanitation in Metropolitan Manila and such contiguous areas as may be added to its area of jurisdiction, and; 1 Lapong, E. & Fujihara M. 2008. Water Resources in the Philippines: An Overview of its Uses, Management, Problems, and Prospects. Journal of Rainwater Catchment Systems. d) National Irrigation Administration (NIA), a government agency under the Office of the President primarily responsible for irrigation development and management. Under the policy of the state to recognize, protect, realize, and enhance the right of all Filipinos to safe, clean, affordable, and accessible drinking water, sanitation, and irrigation, it is the government must streamline the management of these resources. The creation of the Department of Water Irrigation, Sewage, and Sanitation Resource, Management shall address the challenges arising from the fragmented, overlapping, and uncoordinated management of these resources which are presently lodged with various agencies. The water crisis which hit Metro Manila in early 2019 was a wake-up call for all of us. It showed us how inconvenient life can be without a stable supply of water. People were waiting in lines just to get a bucket of this basic necessity. Without water, many of our constituents had difficulty continuing with their daily routine. It became difficult for many to work and study. It is high time we create a department tasked to ensure our people never experience the same inconvenience again. I acknowledge House Bill No. 9176 filed by Hon. Dakila Carlo E. Cua during the 17th Congress upon which this proposed measure was based. I thank Representative Cua for all the good he had done for our country. I hope my inputs in this measure do justice to the version initially filed by the former Representative. On behalf of the people of Parañaque City’s Second District, and for the common good of the Filipino people, the approval of this measure is earnestly sought. REP. GUSTAVO S. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATES, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATINGS FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE It is imperative that the State provide a mechanism to facilitate the effective, efficient and comprehensive use of water resources by the people. Water is a finite resource required for different purposes. El Nifio and climate change affecting the availability of water supply for all must be addressed to prevent water shortages in some areas and extreme flooding in others. With this mechanism in place, these nagging issues can be effectively addressed since the Philippines is one of the countries that claim abundant water supply with its numerous water bodies able to provide an annual renewable water resource of about 146 billion cubic meters, 98% of which originates from surface, and only 28% is being utilized. Presently, however, while the National Water Resources Board (NWRB) under Presidential Decree No. 424 as amended is mandated to manage water resources, control, supervise and regulate the utilization, exploitation, development and protection of water resources, it is ill-equipped to perform its functions. On policy and program coordination, the agency has difficulties in networking with all the agencies engaged in water-related programs. The NWRB’s data on water resource assessment has never been updated since 1980. It does not have the capability on scientific modeling and computerized decision support systems that will aid decision makers and planners in the optimal management of water resources. Many of the agencies sharing the discharge of common functions of water management may be complimentary or sometimes conflict with others with limited oversight and coordination. This may lead to a breakdown in the delivery of water, one of the many basic services by the government. This proposed bill seeks to implement a clear, sustainable, more efficient and effective water resources development and management for the general welfare by establishing the Department of Water Resources. This central agency will be responsible for the comprehensive and integrated identification and mapping of all water resources, planning, policy formulation, and management of the ownership, appropriation, utilization, exploitation, development sustainability and protection of water resources in the Philippines, except fisheries or aquaculture. _ This bill was filed during the 17" and 18 Congresses but due to time constraints no further action was taken on it. It is re-filed for the consideration of the 19" Congress. _ Support for.the enactment of this measure is earnestly requested. REP. Ree RUTH R. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This legislation seeks the creation of the Department of Water Resources as the primary government agency for the management of water utilities in the country. When President Ferdinand R. Marcos, Jr. addressed this Congress during his first State of the Nation Address, he stressed on the importance of coordination and cooperation between government agencies and private entities and stakeholders. Further, he instructed that the organizational structure of the government must be inquired at in order to guarantee its full efficiency. Today, it appears however that several government agencies still perform similar functions and responsibilities, resulting to the unnecessary overlapping of jobs. Looking into several agencies, units and entities that handle the management of water utilities, the country has the Local Water Utilities Administration, the National Irrigation Administration, the National Water Resources Board, the Laguna Lake Development Authority, as well as the DENR, the DPWH, the DOH, the DOST, and the DOE, to name a few. The obvious overlapping and duplication of functions on the management of water utilities create a cloud of confusion as to which department handles the multitude of concerns thereto. In effect, the needed government action could not be expedited since we have to point our fingers first. In 2019, representatives filed 35 separate bills that would create a “Department of Water Resources” (DWR), resulting in a consolidated bill, the House Bill (HB) No. 4944, authored by Albay Rep. Jose Maria Clemente “Joey” Salceda and was approved by the House committees on government reorganization and public works and highways in November 2019. House Biil No. 4944 aspired to make the DWR as the primary government agency to handle the management of water utilities. This representation shares the same vision for a Department that will oversee and streamline the management of water resources and utilities in the country. In this proposed legislation, the Department will serve as the unified agency that will absorb all the functions and duties related to the management of water resources which are currently scattered from among several government agencies and entities. With this bill, significant improvements could be expected in managing this important water sector, such as the reduction of costs for both the government and regulated entities, the avoidance of 2 duplication of functions, and the reconciliation of differences in agencies exercising related responsibilities. This Department aims to create regulatory synergy rather than dysfunction - and this shall serve as one of our responses to the call of the President for coordination and cooperation between government agencies. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. Hon. Jeffeyson F. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In 2015, the Philippines, along with all United Nations Member States, adopted the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. At its center are the 17 Sustainable Development Goals, a call for action by all countries to end poverty and other deprivations while tackling climate change and preserving the natural environment. Of the 17 goals, Sustainable Development Goal 6 aims to ensure the availability and sustainable management of water and sanitation for all. Based on the latest country snapshot, the Philippines needs to accelerate its efforts to achieve the targets under Goal 6. After five years of implementation, progress has been slow with only 47% of the population using a safely managed drinking water service, 61% of the population using a safely managed sanitation service, and 82% of the population having a handwashing facility with soap and water at home. In terms of Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM), the Philippines reported moderate gains in increasing its degree of implementation from 51% in 2017 to 560/o in 2020. However, the Philippines will still need to fast-track refoms to come closer to the 100% target by 2030. In particular, the Philippines will have to allocate more resources and improve coordination between water-related initiatives to strengthen its implementation of IWRM. This bill proposes to improve the implementation of IWRM in the country through the creation of a Department of Water Resources that shall be the primary agency responsible for water policy in the country. In addition, the bureaucracy will be streamlined to support the adoption of IWRM as the strategic framework for national water management, policymaking, and planning. With the creation of the Department of Water Resources, more attention will also be given to the funding requirements of water-related initiatives in the country. This measure was filed in the 18th Congress by Representatives Estrellita 8. Suansing, Horacio P. Suansing, Alfred D. Vargas, Rosanna "Ria" Vergara, Bemadette "BH" Herrera-Dy, Rufus 8. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATES, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATINGS FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Water is life’s most critical resource and is intrinsically considered a fundamental human right. Article II, Section 15 of the 1987 Constitution mandates the State to protect and promote the right to health of the people and instill health consciousness among them. Yet in many parts of the Philippines, people endure inadequate and intermittent access to water supply and sanitation services. The World Health Organization estimates that around 1 in 10 Filipinos do not have access to improved water sources.1 Meanwhile, data from a global non-profit organization revealed that “more than 3 million people in the Philippines depend on unsafe and unsustainable water sources, and 7 million lack access to improved sanitation,”2 making diarrhea one of the leading causes of death in the country.3 Population growth, rapid urbanization, and climate change hazards such as heat waves, drought, storm surges, and floods will continuously exacerbate pressures on our water resources. These entail compounding ramifications to the general welfare of the public and national development. There is therefore an urgent need to put in place a system that would effectively address the critical weaknesses of our water and sanitation management (WSM) sector including challenges arising from the multiple and fragmented institutions governing it. The current institutional regulatory framework of our WSM sector is weak in terms of coherence and clarity of purpose. At present, management of water resources in the Philippines is shared by more than 30 agencies both at the national and local levels such as the National Water Resources Board (NWRB), Local Water Utilities Administration (LWUA), Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS), National Irrigation Administration (NIA), among others. Such has resulted in duplication of functions, constrain in planning, overlapping policies, imbalance in water resource distribution, and even conflicts in implementing programs and policies which ultimately affect the efficiency of the delivery of water and sanitation services to our people. The goal of the bill is to provide an integrated and interdisciplinary approach to address the issues plaguing our WSM. This bill proposes to rationalize the regulation of water resources by the creation of the Department of Water Resources which shall be the primary agency 1 https://www.who.int/philippines/news/feature-stories/detail/water-shortage-in-the-philippines-threatens- sustainable-development-and-health 2 https://water.org/our-impact/where-we-work/philippines/ 3 https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/download?doi=10.1.1.544.3015&rep=rep1&type=pdf responsible for the comprehensive and integrated identification and mapping of all water resources. The Department shall be responsible for planning, policy formulation, and management of the ownership, appropriation, utilization, exploitation, development, and protection of water resources in the Philippines in accordance with the Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM) Framework. The bill also encourages responsible participation of the private sector as an alternative source for financing our water utilities and promotes the establishment of innovative infrastructure and public works that address the challenges of climate change and accelerate universal access to safe, adequate, affordable, and sustainable water supply and improved sanitation services. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. LUIS RAYMUND “LRAY” F. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND CREATING THE DEPARTMENT 0F WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATES, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATINGS FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article 11, Sec.15 of the 1987 Constitution provides that: aThe State shall protect and promote the right to health of the people and instill health consciousness among them." lt is the State's duty to provide safe, clean, accessible, and affordable drinking water, sanitation, and irrigation service to the public. It is of utmost importance that this is achieved through a well-coordinated, effective, efficient, and sustainable management of its water and sanitation resources. According to the 2019 World Water Development Report of the United Nations, 2 billion people live in countries with high water stress level and about 4 billion experience severe water scarcity at least one month in a year. The World Health Organization (WHO) reported that water scarcity affects four out of ten people in the world. World Vision stated that 800 children under the age of five die of diarrhea, every day, which is attributed to poor water and sanitation. A 2015 World Resources Institute study warned that the Philippines will likely experience a "severe water shortage" in the year 2040. This is not surprising given the fact that in the World Bank's 2003 Philippine Environment Monitor, jt was already reported that as of year 2000, compared to other countries in Southeast Asia, the Philippines already ranked 2nd to the lowest in terms of annual renewable water resources per capita. Access to safe and potable drinking water as a basic right was recognized by the United Nations as one of its Millennium Development Goals (MDGs). In July 28, 2010, 122 countries formally acknowledged this "right to water" in a UN General Assembly. Barely two months later, the lTN Human Rights Council adopted a binding resolution recognizing that the human right to water and sanitation is part of the right to adequate standard of living. Our country has been having recurring water shortages and droughts brought about by demand and supply factors and exacerbated by natural calamities, extreme weather events, global warming, and climate change. Population growth, migration, urbanization, and technological advancds weigh in as demand drivers, while environmental factors influence supply. t'/' There have also been seasonal, occasional, and sometimes artificial supply shortages of fish and other seafood, affected by the same demand and supply factors that affect water resources, and result in compromising food security and raising prices of water and food sourced from the inland waters, the seas, and the Pacific Ocean. More than 10 million people in the Philippines still get their water from unsafe sources. As to sanitation, more than 6 million people still lack access to proper sanitation facilities. The country has excess rainwater in the rainy months and acute water needs in the dry months. Meanwhile, the national government has many different agencies attending to compartmentalized although related water and fisheries concerns but lacks a coherent water and fisheries policy framework. These agencies were created one by one to address issues and problems as they arose over the many past decades. Neglected was the rationalization of the alphabet soup of agencies. It seeks to establish a body that shall ensure safe, adequate, affordable, and sustainable water supply and improved sanitation services for all Filipinos and that this finite resource will be sustained. Following the lead of other countries who have found it wise to create a special department to manage this vital resource of water including Japan, Australia, China, and India, the availability of potable water in the Philippines and the continuing water supply for domestic, agricultural and industrial consumption may be ensured and the perennial problem that seriously affects the lives of the people in terms of health, sanitation, food security, and livelihood may be effectively addressed. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In 2019, the World Health Organization released a report stating that 1 in 3 people worldwide do not have access to safe drinking water, or roughly 2.2-billion people who do not have safely managed drinking water services.' It is also estimated that 4.2 billion people do not have safely managed sanitation services, and 3 billion lack basic handwashing facilities. This is an unfortunate situation, given that the United Nations General Assembly explicitly recognized through Resolution 64/292 (28 July 2010) the human right to water and sanitation.* The Resolution also recognized that clean drinking water and sanitation are fundamental to the realization of all human rights. Likewise, the 1987 Constitution provides that the State shall protect and promote the right to health of the people and instill health consciousness among them. (Art. II, Sec. 15) Thus, it is the duty of the State to ensure that safe, quality, and sustainable supply of water, and access to sanitation services, are readily available to the public. Hence, it is endeavored to establish a national framework for resource management of water. This is to ensure the sustainability of the Philippines’ natural resources, especially water, for the generations to come. It is also ideal - in the mission of providing safe, quality, and sustainable water supply and access to sanitation services for all - that a focal department or agency steers the Philippines to the realization of that goal. For this reason, a department of water resources shall be the primary agency which will carry out the planning, policy formulation, and management of the utilization, exploitation, development, and protection of water resources in the country, among other powers and functions. This commendable bill had been filed in the past Congress and the present proponent is acknowledging the wisdom and hard work of his predecessors. All water belongs to the State which shall govern its development and utilization for the people. 10 11 It is hereby declared the policy of the State to ensure the provision of safe, adequate, affordable, and sustainable water supply and improved sanitation services, while maintaining the protection, preservation, and revival of the quality of the country’s water resources and ecological balance. 16 17
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Water access is a fundamental human right. However, all water is the property of the State, which will control how it is developed and used. This bill creates the Department of Water Resources, which is mandated to ensure the best possible use of water resources for domestic and municipal water supply, sanitation, irrigation, hydropower, industry, navigation, flood management, and recreation. Among other salient parts, the Department shall be the primary agency responsible for comprehensive and integrated identification and mapping of all water resources, planning, policy formulation, and management of ownership, appropriation, utilization, exploitation, development, and protection of water resources in the Philippines. Likewise, the Department will also be the primary organization in charge of developing plans and policies to ensure that every Filipino has access to safe, sufficient, affordable, and sustainable water and better sanitation services. The Department will perform the duties and exercise the authority formerly held by the Pasig River Rehabilitation Commission. This measure will streamline the processes that balance utilization and conservation of our precious water resources. Hence, the passage of this measure is sought. RUDYS CAESAR G. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This measure aims to ensure and speed up universal access to water supply and sanitation services by giving priority to infrastructure and public works that can stand up to the effects of climate change and by making it easier for the private sector to get involved. It does this by creating the Department of Water Resources, the Water Pollution Adjudication Board, the National Water Sector Policy Board, and the Water Regulatory Commission. These four groups will take over the powers and functions related to water that are now handled by about 30 different government agencies and bodies. This will make doing business easier. The Department of Water Resources will be the main agency in charge of mapping all water resources, planning, making policies, and taking care of their ownership, use, exploitation, development, protection, and sustainability. Aside from approving the National Water Resources Management Framework Plan, the National Water Policy Board, shall act as a policy advisory body to the President on all things relating to water management and supply, including the declaration of a state of calamity in areas affected by water supply. The Water Regulatory Commission will inherit the economic regulatory functions of the MWSS, NWRB, LWUA, SBMA, PEZA, and TIEZA and exercise quasi-judicial functions to properly carry out the mandates of their office. On July 28, 2010, the United Nations General Assembly declared access to safe and clean drinking water and sanitation to be a human right. With global warming, pollution, and a rising population, posing a major threat to this right, the need to adopt Integrated Water Resource Management as a national framework for planning, policymaking, and management of our water resources is paramount. In light of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa Serbisyong Tinuoray, the undersigned urges the immediate approval of this bill. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE We are surrounded by water. In fact, almost seventy percent (70%) of the earth’s surface is covered with water. Two percent (2%) of it, is freshwater. However, only one percent (1%) of our freshwater can be accessed. The rest is trapped in snowfields and glaciers. This tiny fraction of accessible freshwater caters to around 6.8 billion people. According to the World Health Organization (WHO) and the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), “2.2 billion people lack access to safely managed drinking water services, almost 2 billion people depend on health care facilities without basic water services, and 297,000 children under five die from diarrheal disease, every year, due to poor sanitation, poor hygiene, or unsafe drinking water.” In the 2021 Report of the United Nations – Water, 2.3 billion people live in countries with water stress level, of which 733 million are in high and critically water-stressed countries. Around seventy percent (70%) of the world’s water withdrawal is supplied to agriculture. However, based on the 2020 Report of the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), 3.2 billion people from agricultural areas suffer from water scarcity, 1.2 billion of whom are in severely water-stressed areas. Water stress basically means that the demand for safe and usable water exceeds the supply. The Philippines is in a near-crisis water situation. Several areas in the country suffer from water shortage and intermittent water supply. Metro Manila severely suffered a two-week water crisis in 2019. According to Water.Org, 3 million Filipinos rely on unsafe water sources. One out of ten Filipinos do not have access to safe water sources, based on a study conducted of the WHO. The Philippine Journal of Science published a study stating that three (3) years from now, seventeen (17) out of the twenty (20) major river basins in the country will experience water shortage. We heavily rely on our surface and ground water sources for household and industrial use. The growing population, rapid urbanization and accelerated economic development increase the demand for water supply. The competing demands of agriculture and industries induce water stress and deplete the aquifers. Additionally, pollution, watershed degradation, indiscriminate land use plan and climate change affect our water quality and quantity. Most of our urban rivers are now heavily polluted. In fact, fifty (50) major rivers are now considered biologically dead. It is, therefore, imperative that we prepare for this impending crisis. We need a sustainable and effective development and management plan for our limited water resource. We need the necessary infrastructures to bring our plans into fruition. Water is essential. As a matter of fact, water is life. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this Bill is earnestly, sought. HON. LORDAN G. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The state is directly responsible for providing water security to all the citizens and inhabitants of its territory. Water nurtures and sustains life. Civil societies worldwide can neither endure nor survive without property managing their water resources for the effective use of their people. The philippines is a water-rich country. According to the world Bank (2015), the annual available water volume per capita in the country is twice that of Asia and six times the global scarcity threshold. Yet, many of our people are deprived of efficient access to affordable, safe, and reliable potable water and to proper sanitation services. This is because the governance and maintenance of our water resources remains fragmented and uncoordinated. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to create a Department of Water Resources and Water Regulatory Commission and an Integrated Water Regulatory Commission. Access to potable and sanitary water is still our country’s problem. Tens of millions of Filipinos would still get their water from unclean and contaminated water. Moreover, sanitation facilities are still proven lacking to millions of Filipino homes. Consequently, they are vulnerable to water-related illnesses. It also affects livelihoods of our fisherfolk as polluted waters brought by lack of sanitation facilities would cause red tides and fish kills. Governance and maintenance of our water resource remains fragmented and uncoordinated, which contributed to our problem of unpotable and unsanitary water. Thus, there is a need of a department, which shall serve as the primary agency responsible for national policy- making, coordination, and management of all the water resources in the Philippines. All government agencies related to water shall be rationalized under this Department. Meanwhile, the Integrated Water Regulatory Commission shall enforce effective and adequate delivery of water and sanitation services throughout the country under a coverage or framework of quality and performance targets. It must be emphasized that another problem to be addressed is the water supply level of service and quality of service, which this Commission shall address. Thus, this proposed measure seeks to create a Department of Water Resources and Water Regulatory Commission and an Integrated Water Regulatory Commission. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is most urgently and earnestly recommended. SANDRO L. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The need for the optimum use of water resources has never been more evident in modern times than it is today. Water allocation simply described as the field of managing of water resources is multi-faceted with many current and future issues exacerbated with the growing uncertainties of climate change and the long-term consequences of previous management actions. This bill therefore seeks the creation of a Department of Water Resources as the agency of government that is responsible for the national policies, its implementation and management of all the water resources in the country. All other government agencies whose mandates involve the regulation, management and development of all water resources, water-related functions shall be rationalized under this Department. An Integrated Water Resources Management Plan shall be provided to serve as the strategic framework for policy-making and planning. An independent Water Regulatory Commission is also hereby proposed to ensure that the rights and welfare of consumers are protected under a transparent and accountable regulatory framework for the effective and adequate delivery of water and sanitation services. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this measure is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR WATER RESOUCE MANAGEMENT AND CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATE, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is a water rich country. The Philippines has total annual renewable water resources of 479 billion cubic meters (m3). This Is equivalent to an annual per capacity availability of 6,100 m3, which is twice that of the rest of Asia and six (6) times the global scarcity threshold of 1,000 m3. However, many Filipinos experience deprivation of affordable, safe drinking water and a working sanitation system despite our abundant freshwater sources. The Department of Environment and Natural Resources once stated that the government "...still scrambles to avert a water crisis during the summer season or when the country experiences the El Nino phenomenon." This was most recently seen In the water crises of March 2018, which caused shortages throughout the east zone of Metro Manila, and of March 2019, which cut off the water supply for about ten thousand households across Metro Manila. The Philippines also lacks a strong liquid In-liquid out system. This means that even if households are serviced with clean drinking water, a minute number receive adequate sanitation and sewerage services. This leads to severe cases of leptospirosis, dengue, typhoid, and related tropical and water-borne illnesses. About 31% of illnesses in the country are water-related due to a lack of clean drinking water supply and efficient sanitary facilities. This perennial problem has seriously affected the lives of our citizens in terms of health, sanitation, food security, and livelihood, in addition to negatively impacting the environment. This particularly impacts the poor, who not only have the worst access to water but are also usually compelled to pay more for it. The lack of sufficient, safe, acceptable, accessible, affordable drinking water and sanitation is not unique to the Philippines. However, as the World Water Council has repeatedly stated. It is Incumbent on each country to push for strong standards within its government and contribute to global governance on the issues of water and sanitation. There are many water-related laws in the Philippines. However, their enforcement Is weak and the water sector is beset with problems including poor database and weak cooperation among water agencies, regulatory bodies and local government units (LGUs). There are currently four (4) major economic regulatory agencies for water: the National Water Resources Board (NWRB), the Local Water Utilities Administration (LWUA), LGUs, and national agencies which include Industrial Zones and the Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS). The regulatory framework for water has many overlaps, and economic regulations are provided under a number of different arrangements which result in the framework's instability and fragmentation. Such fragmentation has had significant Implications in the effective and adequate delivery of water and sanitation services in the country. Because there is no lead agency in the water resource sector, the different coordination systems, functions and jurisdictions of the various agencies have made it impossibly hard for water and sanitation to be collectively managed. Thus, the establishment of a unified agency that would focus on water, sewerage and sanitation is certainly very important. This bill seeks to rationalize the economic as well as administrative regulation of water utilities through an independent, quasi-judicial body called the Water Regulatory Commission. Among Its functions are to set the policy for water supply, sewerage and septage management; issue licenses; set, review and approve rates; review and suspend contracts; initiate investigations on erring officials through its quasl-judiclal nature; review and revoke issuances, memoranda and the like, that are not in accordance with the spirit of the Commission, and ensure that the welfare of consumers are prioritized. Similarly, the bill creates a new government agency called, the Department of Water Resources which shall be the primary policy, planning, coordinating, implementing, monitoring, and administrative entity of the executive branch of the government. It shall also be responsible for the comprehensive and integrated development and management of the water resources of the Philippines, and their optimal allocation among competing uses, towards achieving universal access to safe, adequate, and affordable water supply, sanitation, and septage services. To live In a community that is clean, free from human waste, and abundant with safe and affordable drinking water Is an utmost human right, so much so that the United Nations General Assembly explicitly recognized the Right to Water and Sanitation through UN Resolution 64/292 in 2010. To ensure Filipinos the benefit of this most fundamental human right, the urgent approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ^ jf GRACE FOE §>enste of tijc NINETEENTH CONGRESS OF THE ) REPUBLIC OF THE PHILPPINES ) First Regular Session ) ‘22 JUL-7 P2 31 SENATE S. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND CREATING THE DEPARTI^ENT OF WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATES, POWERS AND FUNCIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Water is one of the most important resources in the world. The Philippines, as an archipelagic country, is gifted with this resource In abundance. However, mismanagement and unsustainable consumption of water continues to be a major predicament of the country. According to the article, "Water shortage in the Philippines threatens sustainable development and health" published by the World Health Organization (WHO) on March 22, 2019, around 1 In 10 people In the Philippines still do not have access to improved watei sources. This results to diseases, serious health consequences, and even death. As stated In the article, "When water is scarce, people are often forced to rely on drinking water sources that may not be safe. They may also lack sufficient water for basic hygiene - to wash themselves and their clothes, and to prevent inferJiion including from foodborne and waterborne diseases. Low or negative water pressure In pipes due to short supply can attract contaminants that will put water quality at risk when the supply Is restored. In addition, limited supply obliges people to store more water. If not handled properly. this will provide more opportunity for mosquitoes to breed and consequently increase the cases of mosquito-borne diseases, such as dengue fever." The government needs to Immediately address these concerns by providing comprehensive and long-term solutions. Congruent with the international efforts under the auspices of the WHO, the concerned government agencies should intensify its efforts to develop and implement water safety planning, to strengthen systems and capacity for drifiking water quality surveillance and monitoring, and to improve water, sanitation, and hygiene. Such endeavor Is consistent with Sustainable Development Goal 6 which seeks to provide clean wate” and sanitation for all. Among the targ^its under this SDG are the achievement of universal and equitable access to safe and affordable drinking water for all; Improvement of water quality by reducing pollution, eliminating dumping and minimizing release of hazardous chemicals and materials, halving the proportion of untreated wastewater and substantially increasing recycling and safe reuse globally; and implementation of integrated water resources management at all levels, including through transboundary cooperation as appropriate. The National Water Act' seeks to rationalize the management of water resources, sewerage, and sanitation through the creation of the Department of Water Resources. The Department shall be the primary agency responsible for the comprehensive and Integrated identification and mapping of all water resources, planning, policy formulatior., and management ot the ownership, appropriation, utilization, exploitation, development, and protection of water resources in the Philippines. The bill also establishes the Water Regulatory Commission which shall be placed under the administrative supervision of the Department of Water Resources. To ensure coherent and coordinated management of water resources, the economic regulatory units and functions of the Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS), National Water Resources Board (NWRB), Local Water Utilities Administration (LWUA), Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority (SBMA), Philippine Economic Zone Authority (PEZA), and Tourism Infrastructure and Enterprise Zone Authority (TIEZA) will be tra nsferred to the Commission. This measure was reported out by the Committees on Government Reorganization, Public Works and Highways, Ways and Means, and Appropriations in the House of Representatives in the IS01 Congress. In view of the foregoing, the swift passage of this measure is highly recommended. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE There are around thirty (30) government agencies existing to regulate the water resources of the country, including the Manila Bay Coordinating Office of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), the water quality management section of the Environmental Management Bureau of the DENR, the water supply sanitation unit of the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG), the flood management planning and sediment functions of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), the Lagima Lake Development Authority (LLDA), the Local Water Utilities Administration (LWUA), the National Irrigation Administration (NIA), and the Metro Manila Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS), among others. The overwhelming competition for jurisdiction over funding and water management makes water resources vulnerable to gross mismanagement and exploitation. As a result, the budget allocated for water management multiplies uimecessarily, and jobs are created superfluously or redundantly. This bill seeks to establish the Department of Water Resources which shall be responsible for the comprehensive and systematic management and development of the country's water resources. Under the proposed measure, the Department shall integrate the different government agencies with water-related functions into the Department of Water Resources. National poHcies, plans, and programs focusing on water sewerage and sanitation shall be formulated, recommended, and implemented to ensure water availability for specific uses. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this measure is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES MANAGEMENT, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Water is a basic human need and access to safe and clean drinking water is a basic human right as recognized by the United Nations. As a national water crisis looms according to a study by the Japan International Cooperation Agency and the Philippines' National Water Resources Board and all major cities of the Philippines have been foreseen to all suffer from water shortage by 2025, it is only imperative and necessary to take a much needed affirmative action to prevent this catastrophe. The Philippines, although an archipelagic country blessed with an abundant source of water including rivers, lakes, river basins, and groundwater reservoirs, has already been experiencing severe water shortage ahead of the forecasted 2025 water crisis due to the impact of rapid population growth, urbanization, pollution, excessive and inefficient use of water, and extended period of dry season brought about by climate change. The water shortage is further aggravated by the overlapping functions of water agencies in the country, not to mention the mismanagement on the part of both private and public regulators. The enactment of a feasible Jong-term solution for the protection of water is necessary to combat the threat of possible water crisis in the future. To ensure adequate availability of water in the future, an efficient and effective management and protection of the country's water sources is a great necessity. This bill, therefore, seeks to create the Department of Water Resources Management, which shall be the primary agency responsible for the comprehensive and integrated water resources development and management in the Philippines. Guided by the integrated water resources management framework and taking into account climate risks, the Department shall exercise such powers and functions needed to review, revise, harmonize and integrate policies and regulations for conservation of water resources and effective management of potable water supply. In managing water resources, the Department shall aim to improve water conservation, increase system efficiencies, and optimize the use of all freshwater in the country including ground water, surface water, rainwater, run-offs, floods, storm water and urban drainage, and treated wastewater to meet various needs. Following the lead of other countries who have found it wise to create a special department to manage this vital resource of water including Japan, Australia, China, and India, the availability of potable water in the Philippines and the continuing water supply for domestic, agricultural and industrial consumption may be ensured and the perennial problem that seriously affects the lives of the people in terms of health, sanitation, food security, and livelihood may be effectively addressed. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. TOL" N. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATES, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine Constitution provides that the State shall protect and promote the right to health of the people and instill health consciousness among them (Article 2, Section 15). Meanwhile, the United Nations General Assembly explicitly recognized the right to safe and clean drinking water and sanitation as a human right that is essential for the full enjoyment of life and all human rights (Resolution 64/292, adopted on July 28, 2010). Despite being an archipelagic country that is abundant with natural water resources, the Philippines is facing a water and sanitation crisis. According to the records of the UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme for Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene and the World Health Organization, only 47.46% of the Philippine population had access to safely managed drinking water in 2020. Meanwhile, only 60.64% of the population had access to safely managed sanitation facilities during the same year. While there are many laws and regulatory agencies on the preservation, management, and utilization of water, both law enforcement and agency cooperation are weak. A sole government body focusing on water resources and management will not only strengthen the implementation of water-related laws, but will do away with ineffective coordination among regulatory bodies. This bill seeks to create the Department of Water Resources, a new government agency that will be primarily responsible for the formulation, recommendation, and implementation of national policies, plans, programs for a systematic and efficient water management, and ensure the availability of water for specific purposes in the country. More specifically, this bill mandates the Department to formulate and implement a National Water Resources Management Plan that adheres to an integrated water resources management framework, and includes a water infrastructure development program. In addition, this bill mandates the creation of a Water Regulatory Commission that shall absorb the regulatory functions of local water districts, the regulatory offices of the Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS), among others. As one of the priority measures of President Marcos, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. Furthermore, the heat of the summer also contributed to the shrinking water level of the dams, which even led water companies to conserve the water supply meant for thousands of people in cities and villages. Warmer temperatures mean that 1 https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/1816034/solve-water-woes-before-el-nino-worsens-house-urged 1 moisture in the soil evaporates at faster rates, and more frequent and severe heatwaves shall exacerbate drought conditions and contribute towards water shortages.2 With all the problems encountered, the country Is currently facing a water crisis. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., last March 2023, recently signed an executive order creating a water resource management office (WRMO) as part of the effort to address the water crisis threatening the country. In his latest SONA, the President even stated that water security deserves our special focus and remains hopeful of the passage of a bill creating the Department of Water.3 Thus, this bill seeks to create the Department of Water Resources Management^ which ultimately aims to provide Filipinos with a better quality of life. In more ways than one, the vision of such a life does and will always include clean and safe water for everyone, including the generations still to come. An integrated water resources management framework shall guide the Department, and they shall exercise the powers and functions necessary for the review, revision, and Integration of all regulations and policies pertinent to the conservation and effective management of water resources and water supply. Under the Department, systems shall be developed towards greater efficacy in optimizing the use of all the freshwater sources in the country as well as in improving water conservation. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought.
